title: Why NYC's AI Moratorium Is an Incredibly Smart Move
author: The Digital Delusion
summary: Building on established research showing calculator-assisted math performance evaporates once the calculator is removed, this piece constructs a general theory of when digital tools help learning versus merely mask its absence, centered on the distinction between 'cognitive offloading' (an expert delegating a task they could do themselves, staying in control the way Cory Doctorow's 'centaur' metaphor describes) and 'cognitive outsourcing' (a novice delegating the very process they were supposed to be learning, becoming a 'reverse-centaur' who merely executes what the machine directs). The author's central and most transferable claim is that the same person can be an offloader in one domain and an outsourcer in another purely as a function of prior knowledge -- asking AI to summarize neuroscience (the author's expertise) is offloading, asking it to summarize car repair (an unfamiliar domain) is outsourcing -- meaning generic 'AI literacy' training cannot solve the problem, since the fix is domain knowledge itself, not familiarity with the tool. Applying this framework to New York City's 2026 moratorium on student AI use, the piece defends the policy on two grounds: it is a temporary, evidence-gathering pause rather than a permanent ban, and the fear that restricting AI now will damage a child's future employability misunderstands what K-12 education is actually for -- not training students on today's specific tools, but building the deep domain knowledge that will let them use whatever unpredictable tools exist decades from now. It closes with a carpentry analogy (carpenters aren't better because they swing a hammer better, but because they understand carpentry) to argue that operating AI is trivial while developing the expertise to use it meaningfully is the actual, difficult work of education.
points: The offloading/outsourcing distinction is portable across any tool, not just AI: the same person is an 'offloader' (in control, able to interrogate the tool's output) in a domain they know deeply, and an 'outsourcer' (a 'reverse-centaur' merely executing what the tool directs) in a domain they don't -- so generic AI-literacy training cannot fix outsourcing, only deeper subject knowledge can.

The calculator research is used as a direct precedent and warning: math performance gains from calculator use evaporate, and even reverse, once the calculator is removed, suggesting the tool was boosting calculator-assisted performance rather than actual learning -- exactly the risk the piece argues generative AI poses at much greater scale.

The defense of NYC's policy hinges on reframing what K-12 education is for: not training students to operate 2026's specific AI tools (which will be obsolete before they enter the workforce), but building the deep knowledge base that lets them meaningfully use whatever unpredictable tools exist decades later.

The carpentry analogy reframes the entire debate's emphasis on tool fluency: carpenters aren't superior because they swing a hammer better, but because they understand the material and structures that make swinging a hammer meaningful -- operating AI is trivial, developing the expertise to use it well is the actual difficult work.
quotes: Several meta-analyses have found that students who learn mathematics using calculators perform better on exams…so long as they retain access to their calculators. Once the calculators are removed, this advantage largely disappears and performance on procedural skills typically reverses.
When experts use a tool to make performance easier, we call this cognitive offloading: and it works because established expertise allows the user to maintain control over the tool.

This is not cognitive offloading -- it's now called cognitive outsourcing: when a tool is used to perform the very process a person is meant to be learning. Whereas offloading is a way to demonstrate expertise, outsourcing typically prevents expertise from developing. Instead of becoming centaurs, novices risk becoming reverse-centaurs: the machine supplies the direction while the human performs the minor tasks required to keep it moving.

The transition from outsourcing to offloading has little to do with training on the machine or developing some generic 'AI literacy'. It depends upon deep knowledge of the field in which the tool is being used.

Carpenters aren't better at construction than I am because they can swing a hammer any better than I can. They are better because they deeply understand carpentry. K-12 does not exist to ensure children know how to operate the tools of today: it exists to ensure that, when confronted with the unpredictable tools of tomorrow, they'll have something meaningful to do with them.
